title: King of kings
hook: He is called king of kings and lord of countless Indras (Jaap 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no mark: the One with no sign, no caste, no lineage, and your line, no mark, no sign. Did you take a badge off someone in your mind? Today, the same stanza turns from what He isn't to what He rules. Day three hundred thirty-four.

Picture Delhi in the late 1600s. The emperor sits in a hall of white marble. His titles take a full breath to read aloud, and one of the oldest of them, from Persian, is shahanshah: king of kings. Courtiers bow to the floor. Coins carry his name. Far to the north, in the hills near Anandpur, a young Guru is writing a hymn. And in its very first stanza he takes that same title, king of kings, and gives it away. Not to any man on any throne. Today: king of kings.
screen: `DELHI, LATE 1600S: A MARBLE HALL.` → `SHAHANSHAH: KING OF KINGS.` → `A GURU GIVES THE TITLE AWAY.`

segments.voice: After the list of absences, the first stanza of Jaap turns. The One is achal moorat, an unmoving form; self-lit, of boundless power. Then comes a line with two great titles in it. Kot indr indraan: lord of millions of Indras. Saahu saahaan: king of kings. Start with Indra. In the old stories of India, Indra is the king of the gods, ruler of a shining heaven, the one who sends the rain. To call the One lord of a single Indra would already be enormous. Jaap says millions of them. Imagine every heaven anyone has ever pictured, each with its own crowned king, and the Timeless One above them all. Then saahu saahaan, the Persian title the emperors used. In one line the Guru gathers the highest ruler of the old Indian heavens and the highest ruler of the Persian-speaking courts, and sets both below the One. Why does that matter? Because a person who believes there is a King above every king stands differently in front of power. Sikhs call the Guru sachcha patshah, the true king, and they bow their heads to the Guru, to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to thrones. Sikh history is full of people who would not bow where their conscience said no, and who paid for it. The line isn't a protest slogan. It's praise. But praise like this changes posture. If the One is above every throne, then every throne on earth is borrowed. And the head you bow in the morning is a head that doesn't need to bow to fear.
screen: `ACHAL MOORAT: THE UNMOVING FORM.` · `LORD OF MILLIONS OF INDRAS.` · `SAAHU SAAHAAN: KING OF KINGS.` · `EVERY EARTHLY THRONE IS BORROWED.` · then, large: `ABOVE EVERY THRONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow your head for a moment. Sit comfortably. Let your chin drop slowly toward your chest, as if you were in a gurdwara, where Sikhs bow their foreheads before the Guru Granth Sahib. Stay there for a few breaths. Notice what a bow feels like from the inside: the neck softening, the eyes lowering, the mind getting quieter. Then lift your head slowly and sit tall. Bowed, then upright. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow. The bell holds the time.
King of kings. Saahu saahaan in the first stanza of Jaap: the One is lord of millions of Indras and above every emperor.
Your line: above every throne. Today, when someone's title or status makes you shrink a little, remember the line, straighten your back, and stay kind. Day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs bow their foreheads to the floor (matha tekna) before the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, and often speak of the Guru as sachcha patshah, the true king.

fork.setup: you are writing praise in an age when the emperor is called king of kings. what does the first stanza of Jaap do with that title?
options: give it to the Timeless One, above every throne.
fork.reveal: Jaap calls the One saahu saahaan, king of kings, and lord of millions of Indras: every ruler, heavenly or earthly, sits below.

original.note: Gurmukhi: patshah, king, from Persian; Sikhs call the Guru sachcha patshah, the true king.

trapdoor: what you thought: king of kings is a grand old phrase.
what it means: the One is above every ruler, lord of millions of Indras, so every earthly throne is borrowed.
what a scholar hears: the line pairs a Puranic figure (Indra, king of the devas) with a Persian court title (shah-e-shahan), setting both beneath Akal.

sources.ref: Indra as king of the gods (Puranic and Vedic tradition)

notes: Transliterations 'achal moorat', 'kot indr indraan', 'saahu saahaan' from Jaap 1: confirm.
The Mughal emperors' use of shahanshah (king of kings) as a title: confirm; the hook does not name the emperor.

Anandpur as the place of composition is not claimed; the hook says 'in the hills near Anandpur, a young Guru is writing a hymn'. Tradition places much of the Dasam Granth's writing at Anandpur and Paonta; confirm or soften.
Gurmukhi ਪਾਤਿਸ਼ਾਹ (patshah) and 'sachcha patshah' as a Sikh title for the Guru: confirm spelling.
